name: Takpa (Retired)
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

sources.citation: Tombleson, Anette Helgestad. 2022. Grammar sketch of Tawang Monpa. Himalayan Linguistics 21(2): 105-141. doi:10.5070/H921252709.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: Sec. 2 Phonology (pp. 106-110) covers consonants, vowels and sec. 2.3 'Tone and vowel length' (pp. 109-110): 'Both tone and vowel length is minimally contrastive in Tawang Monpa, with a two-way high/low tone distinction. Tone is contrastive only after sonorants, while it is predictably high after unvoiced stops, and low after voiced stops.' The words stress/accent do not occur anywhere in the paper (a full-text search for stress/accent = 0).

sources.citation: Bodt, Timotheus A. 2023. East Bodish revisited. Bulletin of Tibetology 54(1): 49-212 (scanned text held); with Bodt 2022 Zenodo data supplement (record 6559623).
sources.note: Comparative-historical; Dakpa varieties (after Lu 1986, 2002) have a high vs. low register tone onset; a full-text search for stress/accent yields no Dakpa stress statement.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.x languoid records takp1246 (Takpa, Bookkeeping; iso_retirement 2010-017 -> twm), tawa1289 (Tawang Monpa, Bookkeeping; Ethnologue comment: dka, tkk, twm are the same language) and dakp1242 (Dakpakha, Sino-Tibetan > Bodish > Dakpa-Dzala); ISO 639-3 code pages for tkk (Deprecated) and twm.
sources.note: Nothing; identity chain only. dakp1242 has 6 descriptive refs (Tombleson 2022 sketch; Wangchu 2002 sketch, 96 pp; Hyslop & Tshering 2008/2010 sketch; Nishida 1989 Gengogaku daijiten entry; Tombleson 2020 copulas).

sources.citation: ISO 639-3 Registration Authority. 2010. Change Request Number 2010-017: retire [tkk] Takpa, merge into Tawang Monpa [twm] (adopted 2011-05-18). SIL International. Submitted by Barb Waugh 2009-12-07, 6 pp.
sources.note: Nothing; sect. 3 (pp. 2-3) is the identity rationale: Takpa = Dwags/Dakpa of Hodgson 1853 and Shafer 1954 = Tawang Monpa [twm] = Cuona Monpa, East Bodish.

sources.citation: van Driem, George. 2007. Dzala and Dakpa form a coherent subgroup within East Bodish, and some related thoughts. In Roland Bielmeier & Felix Haller (eds.), Linguistics of the Himalayas and beyond, 71-84. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.
sources.note: 'Phonological impressionism' (pp. 75-76): 'A thorough phonological analysis of Dzala and Dakpa has not yet been completed'; 'There may, however, be register tone similar to the binary distinction characteristic of Dzongkha phonology'. Silent on stress (only 'acute accent' as a diacritic for creaky/tense vowels).

sources.citation: PHOIBLE inventory 2350 'Northern Cuona' (dakp1242), source Namkung 1996 (STEDT phonological inventories); Wikipedia 'Takpa language' (cites Huang Bufan (ed.) 1992 Zang-Mian yuzu yuyan cihui p. 634 for four tones 55, 53, 35, 31).
sources.note: Segment inventory only, no tones and no stress information (PHOIBLE); Wikipedia: 'Monba is a tonal language, with four contour tones: 55, 53, 35, and 31' after Huang 1992, nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Michailovsky, Boyd & Martine Mazaudon. 1994. Preliminary notes on the languages of the Bumthang group. In Per Kvaerne (ed.), Tibetan Studies (PIATS 6, Fagernes 1992), vol. 2, 545-557. Oslo.
sources.note: Phonology section is on Kurtoep (two tonal registers); Dakpa appears only as comparative wordlist data; nothing on Dakpa stress.

sources.citation: Nishida, Tatsuo. 1988 [1989]. The mTsho-sna Monpa language of China and its place in the Tibeto-Burman family. In David Bradley, Eugenie J.A. Henderson & Martine Mazaudon (eds.), Prosodic analysis and Asian linguistics: to honour R.K. Sprigg, 223-236. Pacific Linguistics C-104. Canberra: ANU. (based on Sun et al. 1980 / Lu 1986 Mama and Wenlang data)
sources.note: pp. 231-233: tones 53/55 (voiceless series, high) vs 35 (voiced series, low) and 31; 'In the case of two-syllable words.. there is a tendency for them to be integrated into two main patterns, that is, a 55-53 type and a 35-53 type.' No mention of stress or accent.

sources.citation: Hyslop, Gwendolyn & Karma Tshering. 2010 [2009]. Preliminary notes on Dakpa (Tawang Monpa). In Stephen Morey & Mark Post (eds.), North East Indian Linguistics vol. 2, 3-21. New Delhi: Foundation Books / CUP India.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: The only modern first-hand phonemic analysis of Tawang Dakpa (2007 fieldwork); Glottolog's top-ranked sketch; a phonemic-inventory section is the most likely place for any statement on stress vs. tone.
